title: The_Supreme_Backdoor_Factory_Incident_Response_Scenario_38a
description: Investigate and respond to a backdoor factory incident involving GitHub-based command and control.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The Supreme Backdoor Factory is a collection of malicious GitHub repositories and accounts used to deliver various payloads. The malware involves the use of GitHub for command and control (C2) purposes, with payloads being delivered through malicious repositories. The behavior includes the creation of scheduled tasks to download and execute PowerShell code from dynamic DNS subdomains. This scenario focuses on investigating and responding to this specific threat actor and malware type.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have been granted access to the target system as user `cyrano` with password `cyrano`. Your initial entry point is the `target` host at IP address `192.168.50.5`. From this host, you can SSH to other systems in the environment using the same credentials.
levels.local_content: You have been granted access to the target system as user `cyrano` with password `cyrano`. Your initial entry point is the `target` host at IP address `192.168.50.5`. From this host, you can SSH to other systems in the environment using the same credentials.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content: Investigate the `target` host for any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system. Enumerate running services and distinguish legitimate from suspicious services.
levels.solution: Run `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all running services. The hidden flag is the name of the suspicious service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the systemd service manager for any unusual services that might not belong to standard system operations.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for services that have unusual names or descriptions.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service name starts with 'payload'.

levels.title: Identify Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Determine how the suspicious service identified in the previous task is automatically started after reboot. Identify persistence mechanisms (e.g., systemd, cron, scheduled task).
levels.solution: Run `systemctl list-timers` to list all systemd timers. The hidden flag is the name of the persistence timer.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Examine the systemd service files and timers to understand how the service is scheduled to run.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for timers that are associated with the suspicious service.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The persistence timer name starts with 'payload'.

levels.title: Analyze Network Connections
levels.content: Investigate the network connections on the `target` host to identify any suspicious communication. Analyze network traffic and identify suspicious ports or connections.
levels.solution: Run `ss -tulnp` to list all active network connections and listening ports. The hidden flag is the C2 port number used for suspicious communication.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Use network monitoring tools to inspect active connections and listen ports.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for connections to unusual or unexpected ports.
